figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic. A-TMLE decomposes the trial-population ATE into a pooled projection Ψ̃ (via the working model τA) minus a bias projection Ψ# (via the learned τS); the efficient influence curve is D = DA − DS . Contribution (1) audits τS (the report card); contribution (2) maps the gain R; contribution (3) builds a calibrated interval for R via the block jackknife.

Table 2: Roadmap of the simulation study. Each component, the question it answers and what it shows, and where to find the headline display in the main text and the full per-cell results in the Supplementary Material (Web Appendices). The three contributions are (1) the report card, (2) the efficiency map, and (3) selection-aware inference.

Table 9: A public-health fusion: the WASH Benefits trial. The randomized WASH Benefits arm (S = 1: 150 treated, 150 control) is augmented with one external study arm (S = 0) — either a deliberately biased or an unbiased arm — to estimate the effect of the water/sanitation/handwashing intervention on child length-for-age Z-score. Rows report the fused and matched RCT-only ATE (standard error), the learned bias-model size, the influencecurve variance attribution, and the efficiency gain with its naive and blockjackknife intervals.

Figure 2: Recovery surface. The learned bias model τ̂S(W,A) (solid, from cross-validated relaxedHAL) against the truth τS,0(W,A) = −B(W,A) (dashed), sliced at W2 = W3 = 0, by treatment arm (A = 0/A = 1, columns) and scenario (rows). The report card reproduces the structure of the enrollment-effect surface, including the arm-specific W1-dependence. Alt text: Grid of line plots. Table 1: The three contributions at a glance. Each is a general methodological/empirical result, instantiated on A-TMLE for RCT+RWD fusion.

Table 10: Two real-data fusions on the National Supported Work demonstration. The randomized NSW job-training trial (S = 1: 185 treated, 260 controls) is augmented with one external observational-controls arm (S = 0, all untreated) to estimate the effect of training on 1978 earnings. The efficiency gain is at or below parity in both fusions — a more biased external arm does not buy efficiency — and the block-jackknife interval for the gain is ∼4× wider than the over-confident naive interval, the Section 4.5 message on real data. A single-dataset illustration, not a coverage assessment.

Table 6: The sub-unity gain survives a stronger reference and erodes with sample size. Panel A: influence-curve gain of A-TMLE against three RCT-only references computed on the same fit; a more efficient reference does not raise the gain (the flexible SuperLearner collapses to the GLM on these near-linear DGPs, and the gain rises only against the noisier relaxed-HAL reference). Panel B : against the efficient (GLM/SL) reference the no-bias gain shrinks toward one and the parity crossing moves to smaller bias as n grows.

Table 3: Report card: recovery of the learned bias model τ̂S. For each bias shape and magnitude m, cor⋆ is the correlation between the targeted learned bias surface and the truth, and d̄ the mean number of active basis terms in the selected working model, over B = 1000 replicates. Recovery is strong where it matters — ≥ 0.82 for every shape once m ≥ 2, ≈ 0.95 for a linear bias — and degrades only at small magnitude, where the true bias is near-constant.

Table 8: A biomedical fusion: the ACTG175 HIV trial. The antiretroviral-naive randomized arm (S = 1: 663 on an alternative regimen, 223 on zidovudine monotherapy) is augmented with one external cohort (S = 0) of antiretroviral-experienced patients to estimate the regimen’s effect on CD4 count at 20 weeks. The external cohort is the same trial’s treatment-experienced stratum, split by prior-antiretroviral burden into a lightly-pretreated arm (closer to the naive trial population) and a heavily-pretreated arm (prognostically more distant), at essentially equal size, so the report-card difference reflects the external cohort rather than its sample size. Rows report the fused and matched RCT-only ATE (standard error), the learned bias-model size, the influence-curve variance attribution, the efficiency gain, and its naive and block-jackknife intervals.

Table 7: Ten selection-aware standard errors for the efficiency gain, scored against a fixed truth. Each method estimates the gain and a standard error of its logarithm; entries are ranges over the 15 cells (Linear/Interaction/Wiggly × m ∈ {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4}), B = 500. Only the block jackknife attains nominal (markedly conservative) coverage; no other method reaches 0.93 in any cell. The gap between the fixed-truth and own-mean coverage columns is itself diagnostic: the cross-fit, winsorized, and CV-TMLE comparators look respectable self-centered yet collapse against the fixed truth. Per-method compute time (all ten) is reported in Web Appendix F: every fold-based SE costs ≈ V A-TMLE fits, so the block jackknife is no more expensive than the variants that fail.
